papers.title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing
papers.abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce BORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. BORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, BORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, BORN finishes in 1.41h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, BORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1,h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1,h (173$\times$).

papers.title: Neural Network Path Optimization for Finding Transition States on a Machine Learned Potential
papers.abstract: Transition states govern chemical reaction rates and outcomes, yet locating them remains a central challenge in computational chemistry. Double-ended search methods find transition states given reactant and product structures, but generally rely on discretized path representations developed for density functional theory, where potential energy surface evaluations are expensive. Machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) dramatically reduce this cost and leverage automatic differentiation to access higher-order derivatives efficiently. We introduce Popcornn, a framework to find transition states by optimizing continuous neural network paths atop an MLIP with a parallelized adaptive numerical integrator. This combination eliminates path discretization artifacts, reduces hyperparameter sensitivity, and enables non-local optimization to overcome local features using second-order potential-energy-surface information. Popcornn consistently recovers more correct transition states than standard methods such as nudged elastic band and growing string, across MLIPs on thousands of organic reactions, establishing it as a robust, automation-ready method for high-throughput transition state search. Popcornn's infrastructure is flexible in path objective, integration strategy, and optimization algorithm, making it a practical tool and platform for investigating open questions in MLIP-based path optimization.

papers.title: A closed-loop framework for perovskite precursor additive discovery
papers.abstract: Efficient discovery of precursor additives is essential for improving the performance of perovskite solar cells, yet the large chemical space makes conventional trial-and-error screening inefficient. Here we show that LEAP (LLM-driven Exploration via Active Learning for Perovskites), a closed-loop framework combining a domain-specialized language model with active learning, prioritizes perovskite precursor additives under low-data conditions. The model extracts mechanism-relevant knowledge from the literature and converts it into interpretable molecular descriptors for uncertainty-aware Bayesian optimization. On an evaluation drawn from unseen literature, the specialized model provides more mechanism-consistent answers than the tested general-purpose models. In an expert-guided proof-of-concept study, two later-round additives increase average device power conversion efficiencies to 20.13% and 20.87%, compared with 19.25% for the control, and the best device reaches 21.32%. Because only a limited number of candidates are tested prospectively, these results provide preliminary evidence that literature-grounded molecular representations, Bayesian optimization, and expert assessment can support additive discovery for perovskite solar cells.

papers.title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
papers.abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.

papers.title: An open dataset of gas adsorption in deformable metal-organic frameworks for direct air capture
papers.abstract: Engineering economical and scalable processes for direct air capture (DAC) from humid air relies on atomistic modeling to search and identify promising sorbent materials from a vast chemical space. Machine learning has emerged as a powerful tool for predicting material properties in an efficient yet accurate manner, but these models require large sets of carefully curated training data. We present the Open DAC 2025 (ODAC25) dataset comprising nearly 60 million DFT single-point calculations for CO2, H2O, N2, and O2 adsorption in ~15,000 MOFs. ODAC25 introduces functionalized MOFs, high-energy adsorbate placements, and synthetically generated frameworks to maximize the versatility of models trained on the dataset. ODAC25 improves upon the accuracy of DFT calculations in previous works and applies engineering intuition from recent work regarding the treatment of adsorbate-induced MOF flexibility. We release state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on ODAC25 and demonstrate their utility via Henry's coefficient predictions. ODAC25 enables MOF screening for DAC at a resolution previously unattainable.

papers.title: Sobolev theory for the inverse problem of time-dependent density functional theory on the torus
papers.abstract: We show that, given a sufficiently regular time-dependent density, there exists a unique potential such that the Schr\"odinger equation with this external potential has the prescribed one-particle density. We treat densities that are twice differentiable in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space; the resulting potentials are continuous in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space. Our method of proof is to rewrite the problem as a nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation with a loss of derivatives, which we in turn handle with a completion-of-the-square argument. This is a refinement of our recent work [Lauritsen, Lewin, and Oldenburg, arXiv:2609.08984], which handled this loss of derivatives using the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem and treated analytic-in-space densities and potentials.

papers.title: Plane partitions and spin adapted quantum states
papers.abstract: We describe an explicit basis for the $\operatorname{SU}(2)$-invariant space of the exterior power $\wedge_{2k} \mathbb{C}^{2m}$ via the combinatorics of plane partitions. In quantum chemistry, this is the space of spin adapted quantum states of an electronic system with $m$ spin orbitals and $k$ electron pairs. We construct our basis by identifying the invariant space with an Artinian commutative ring called the excitation ring. We compute a Gr\"obner basis and enumerate its standard monomials via an explicit bijection to Dyck paths counted by the Narayana numbers.

papers.title: Quantum-classical dynamical density functional theory for solvation dynamics
papers.abstract: We provide a unified modeling framework for thermalization and non-equilibrium spectroscopy in overdamped polar environments. This framework extends dynamical density functional theory to describe the coupled quantum-classical evolution of a molecular electronic subsystem and an overdamped polar solvent represented by a reaction-field coordinate. The nonadiabatic dynamics is formulated in terms of an operator-valued distribution obeying a quantum-classical Ehrenfest--Smoluchowski equation which exhibits nonlinear classical diffusion and non-increasing free energy, thereby retaining detailed balance. In contrast, a quantum-classical Liouville--Smoluchowski model with quantum-classical linear diffusion develops unstable long-time behavior and fails to reach a stationary thermal state. The method is applied to a two-level model of a polar dye in three different solvents: chloroform, dichloromethane, and dimethyl sulfoxide, each differing in polarity and dielectric relaxation time. Absorption and time-resolved emission spectra are obtained from dipole-dipole correlation functions, capturing the solvent-induced spectral broadening, the dynamic Stokes shift, and the time evolution of the emission bandwidth. The calculated solvent spectral response agrees well with the experimental relaxation trends of the three solvents.

papers.title: Mechanically induced self-propagating reactions within the realm of mechanochemistry: Fundamentals, overview, in situ monitoring and perspectives
papers.abstract: Mechanically induced self-propagating reaction (MSR) represents a promising but rather underexplored phenomenon within mechanochemistry, a solvent-free alternative to classical solution-based chemistry. In contrast to the gradual mechanochemical reactions, MSRs are sub-second combustive-like processes bringing about substantial benefits such as faster product formation, time efficiency, and lower energy consumption. Despite the fact that the mechanochemical field is in the research spotlight, MSR investigation remains on the periphery. This review aims to catalyze a renaissance in MSR fundamentals investigation by reviewing the current state-of-the-art. This is done via systematically reviewing the reaction systems that were reported to react via a MSR in the past twenty years, such as metal-metalloid ones (carbides, borides, silicides, and carbonitrides), metal chalcogenides, metal oxides, and other specific types of reactions. A couple of case studies are briefly reviewed for each system, and the comprehensive table follows afterward. The review also revisits the factors impacting the MSR course from milling conditions and reagent's properties point of view, showing either a direct or inverse relationship with MSR ignition time. The recent development in the in situ monitoring of mechanochemical reactions allowed to obtain some mechanistic insights into the MSR process, which are summarized in the last chapter.

papers.title: Temperature Flips the Sign of the Hydrogen Response in Nanogranular Palladium Networks
papers.abstract: In nanogranular palladium networks, hydrogen uptake has two opposing effects on electrical resistance. Absorbed hydrogen scatters electrons within the particles, raising their resistance, while particle expansion narrows the gaps between them and lowers the junction resistance. Such networks are widely studied as resistive hydrogen sensors, and the sign of their net response is usually treated as a fixed property of the architecture. In networks grown by atomic layer deposition on macroporous silicon, we show that changing the operating temperature can reverse this sign at a fixed hydrogen concentration. A thermodynamic model indicates that scattering contributes less as temperature rises, allowing sub-angstroem changes in gap width to dominate. Where the two effects cancel, the network absorbs hydrogen yet gives the same reading as in hydrogen-free gas, so a leak could escape detection. Between 25 and 40 degrees Celsius, this cancellation point is predicted to rise over tenfold, crossing reported leak-alarm setpoints. At 55 degrees Celsius, the measured response stays negative but passes through a minimum, so a concentration above a setpoint can mimic one below it. Annealing at 200 degrees Celsius alters the calibration and turns the room-temperature response negative at the lowest concentration tested. Quantitative sensing therefore requires a defined thermal pretreatment and an operating temperature giving distinct signals across the intended concentration range. Response polarity becomes an operating parameter rather than a fixed property. More broadly, any nanoparticle network whose particles deform on sorption may show the same temperature-dependent competition between transport within and between particles, with implications for sensors and switches beyond palladium-hydrogen.

papers.title: Spin and Orbital Angular Momentum Textures at Chiral Molecule-Metal Interfaces
papers.abstract: Chiral molecular adsorption can modify the spin and orbital character of metal surface states, providing an electronic-structure basis for interpreting spin-dependent interfacial phenomena. Using first-principles calculations with spin-orbit coupling, band unfolding, and an atom-projected orbital angular momentum (OAM) analysis, we investigate spin and OAM textures at chiral heptahelicene/Au(111) interfaces and compare them with clean Au (111) and an achiral coronene/Au system. Adsorption changes the orientations of the spin and OAM vectors and reduces the sampled OAM magnitudes of Au-derived surface states near the Fermi level. The two heptahelicene enantiomers exhibit textures related by mirror and time-reversal symmetries, whereas the comparison with coronene identifies changes that also occur without molecular chirality. These results clarify how molecular adsorption modifies interfacial spin and orbital character and establish symmetry constraints relevant to chirality-dependent photoemission.

papers.title: Symmetry-reduced k-point sampling and Wannier analysis with localized Gaussian orbitals
papers.abstract: Brillouin-zone sampling with localized orbitals requires consistent transformations between sparse real-space matrices and complex Bloch states. Symmetry reduces the number of reciprocal-space problems, but scalar integration weights alone cannot reconstruct the matrices and wavefunctions needed for densities and orbital analysis. We develop a unified formulation of these transformations for nonorthogonal Gaussian bases and describe its implementation in CP2K. Atom permutations, local orbital rotations, and lattice phases connect irreducible-point solutions to full symmetry orbits while preserving the overlap metric. Direct and fast lattice transforms couple this construction to self-consistent calculations, including complex orbital optimization and finite-temperature occupations. Gauge-consistent full-mesh orbitals and directed inter-point overlaps support Wannier90 export, Wannier construction, and Hamiltonian interpolation. In silicon and aluminium tests, symmetry reduces a 64-point mesh to four representatives while retaining cell energies or electronic free energies within $1.5\times10^{-12}$ hartree of the unreduced calculation. Hybrid exchange and many-body applications illustrate the additional role of auxiliary bases and transfer momenta. The resulting framework connects symmetry-reduced integration to gauge-consistent analysis of periodic electronic states within a localized-orbital representation.

papers.title: Orbital differentiation in a rare earth ion near half filling
papers.abstract: In the electronic structure of rare earth ions, details can be crucial for understanding the origin of correlated states. Currently, state-of-the-art wavefunction-based methods (e.g. CASSCF) can capture single-ion properties of molecular magnets and some band insulating systems, but are expensive to perform, and cannot be applied to metallic systems. Here, we carry out full multiplet calculations for SmN with the cubic rock-salt structure using the crystal field software Quanty. The calculated experimental observables from our model agree precisely with magnetic susceptibility and inelastic neutron scattering experiments, and the spatially resolved spin density also agrees with DFT predictions. By tuning the crystal field parameters, our full multiplet-derived wavefunctions reveal the presence of orbital differentiation of the ground $J=\frac{5}{2}$ manifold into two groups, which are distinct subspaces with different orbital stiffness. This violation of Hund's rule, observed with a fast and inexpensive calculation tool, represents a step forward for microscopic models of rare earth materials, and may provide support for the claim of unconventional triplet superconductivity in SmN.

papers.title: When Do Tensor Product Paths Matter? A Group-Theoretic Analysis of Equivariant Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Tensor-product (TP) layers in equivariant interatomic potentials encode angular interactions through symmetry-allowed paths. Yet local site symmetry can make an allowed path carry no signal after neighbor aggregation. We call this effect Aggregation Cancellation. In a scalar-input first layer, equal-species neighbors on a complete site-symmetry orbit share scalar and radial factors, reducing their angular contribution to a spherical-harmonic orbit sum. If the restricted degree-$l$ representation has no trivial component, this sum and the corresponding path vanish for any learned radial weight. For an ideal $O_h$ octahedral orbit, this removes the $l_\mathrm{edge}=1,2,3$ classes. Beyond the first layer, the factorisation no longer holds, so cancellation is no longer guaranteed; we instead ask whether affected paths remain less important on average. We test the two levels separately in NequIP: matched-radius TiO$_6$ probes examine first-layer cancellation, whereas a within-model CaTiO$_3$ comparison and six OMat24 models examine the importance bias. We then rank paths on training frames, choose the pruning fraction on validation frames, and evaluate frozen masks on held-out tests. At the highest evaluated fraction (60% of 174 paths), force mean absolute error (MAE) changes are 1.42%, 0.04%, and 1.83% for CaTiO$_3$, OMat24 $O_h$-cubic, and OMat24 low-symmetry data, respectively. The masks imply 67.12-71.94% potential TP-operation reduction and 59.77% potential edge multilayer perceptron (MLP) reduction; these are structural proxies, not measured speedups. The results connect local symmetry to path redundancy and pruning robustness in NequIP; transfer to other architectures remains open.

papers.title: Multicomponent Adaptive Sampling Configuration Interaction method in openLOWDIN: positronic and quantum nuclear systems
papers.abstract: We present a multicomponent Selective Configuration Interaction (SCI) method based on the deterministic Adaptive Sampling CI (ASCI) algorithm for computing energies and wavefunction properties of molecular systems containing leptons of variable masses, or quantum nuclei. Near-FCI accuracy is achieved by incorporating second-order Epstein-Nesbet perturbation theory or by dressing the Hamiltonian via Davidson's and co-workers shifted-Bk method. We validate the approach through benchmark positronic (e$^+$LiH, e$^+$OH$^-$, e$^+$Mg) and quantum nuclear systems (HCN), establishing a novel protocol for accurate convergence, based on the iterative adaptation of natural orbitals starting from those obtained by considering only cross-particle CISD excitations, to those obtained from SCI variational space, surpassing the accuracy of previous SCI studies. Overall, we show that the present multi-component SCI framework offers a simple, systematically improvable, and cost-effective alternative to traditional CI approaches.

papers.title: Accelerating auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo with mixed-precision random propagators
papers.abstract: We develop an algorithm to propagate auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) wavefunctions in mixed precision. We target NVIDIA Tensor Cores using the TensorFloat-32 (TF32) format. We approximate each full-precision array by a TF32 leading term and a TF32 residual, and each full-precision matrix product by three TF32 products accumulated in full precision. Benchmarks on hydrogen chains show that mixed-precision propagation is consistently faster than double-precision GPU propagation, with an increasing advantage as the system size grows. The resulting local-energy deviations remain small over the propagation windows considered here. These results identify the stochastic two-body propagator as a particularly effective target for reduced precision, while our method allows higher precision to be retained for accuracy-sensitive operations. Hence, our algorithm provides a practical way to speed up AFQMC calculations and demonstrates where reduced precision can be applied without adverse effects on the method's accuracy.

papers.title: Efficient strategies for obtaining accurate kinetics from biased simulations
papers.abstract: It has been demonstrated that one can recover the unbiased rate constants for slow conformational transitions by observing transitions driven by a bias potential added along one or several collective variables (CVs). However, the choice of CV, biasing scheme, biasing parameters and the rate estimator can all affect the results and it is not obvious which to choose for a given problem. In this study, we compare accuracy versus computational cost for a previously established benchmark system, a coarse-grained protein with computationally accessible unfolding kinetics. We apply bias to four CVs of decreasing quality in both a time-dependent and quasi-static manner, and compare different estimators for the unfolding rate constant in terms of absolute accuracy to the estimated reference unbiased rate. We show that in the case of gentle biasing, the exponential average time-dependent rate (EATR) framework, which simultaneously fits the unbiased rate constant and a coordinate quality metric $\gamma$, recovers accurate kinetics in nearly all cases.For poor CVs, estimators equivalent to assuming a good coordinate ($\gamma=1$) systematically fail regardless of biasing method or parameters. We introduce heuristics to show when we expect the rates to be inaccurate, and identify which combinations of biasing scheme, estimator and number of runs reach a given accuracy at the lowest cost.

papers.title: Spin-free potential-energy curves, spectroscopic constants, and permanent dipole-moment functions for all 18 CO states correlating with the first atomic asymptote
papers.abstract: We report ab initio potential-energy curves and permanent dipole-moment functions for all 18 spin-free adiabatic electronic states of $^{12}$C$^{16}$O correlating with the lowest dissociation limit, C($^3$P)+O($^3$P). Our state-averaged CASSCF/icMRCI(+Q) calculations with the aug-cc-pV5Z basis cover the complete set of singlet, triplet, and quintet manifolds. For the ground state, we examine basis-set convergence using the aug-cc-pV$n$Z series ($n=T,Q,5,6$) and extrapolate to the complete-basis-set limit. The resulting potential-energy curves reproduce the established topology of the low-lying CO states, including the double-minimum structure of the 2$^{1}\Sigma^{+}$ state and pronounced adiabatic mixing in several excited states. We determine rovibrational levels and spectroscopic constants for bound states and selected local minima, assess uncertainties, and compare our results with experiment and previous calculations. We find good agreement with experiment for the ground state and well-characterized low-lying singlet and triplet states. For the $1^1\Sigma^+$ ground state, $R_e=1.131~\r{A}$ and $\omega_e=2161.04$~cm$^{-1}$ are both within $0.5\%$ of experiment. The dissociation energy is $D_0=89473\pm141$~cm$^{-1}$. The most strongly bound quintet, $1^5\Pi$, has $D_e=6401$~cm$^{-1}$ and $\omega_e=982~$cm$^{-1}$. The $1^5\Sigma^+$ state has a shallow long-range well with $D_e=849$cm$^{-1}$, while $2^5\Sigma^+$, $2^5\Pi$, and $1^5\Delta$ are predominantly repulsive. Variations in the permanent dipole moments with bond length indicate changes in electronic character and charge redistribution, particularly where adiabatic states interact strongly. These data provide a basis for interpreting rovibrational spectra and for future studies of nonadiabatic effects, spin--orbit coupling, and collision dynamics.

papers.title: Collisional lineshapes of an N$_2$-perturbed electronic transition in O$_2$ from first principles of quantum theory validated by accurate experimental spectra
papers.abstract: We demonstrate the feasibility of predicting the lineshape of an electronic molecular transition collisionally perturbed by another molecule from first principles of quantum mechanics. We consider an N$_2$-perturbed O$_2$ $A$-band transition, which is relevant to spectroscopic observations in Earth's atmosphere. This approach simultaneously incorporates the electronic structure, quantum scattering and lineshape effects required to accurately predict pressure- and temperature-dependence of observed lineshapes. The $\textit{ab initio}$ lineshapes reproduce measurements to better than 0.6%. Theory also provides new physical constraints on beyond-Voigt lineshape parameters in fits of high-precision data, yielding fit residuals at the 0.08% level. This work motivates advances in molecular electronic structure calculations and demonstrates the potential to generate comprehensive spectroscopic reference data from first principles.

papers.title: Quadrature-Free Radial Intracule Densities: A Bessel-Harmonic Formulation for Gaussian Basis Sets
papers.abstract: The radial intracule density $I(R)$, the probability distribution of the interelectronic distance, is a compact and physically transparent picture of electron correlation, but its evaluation for molecules has always relied on a numerical angular quadrature over the orientation of the interelectronic vector. We show that this quadrature can be removed altogether for Cartesian Gaussian basis sets and arbitrary second-order density matrices. Starting from the Hermite Gaussian expansion of the products of basis functions, the coupling exponential $e^{2\mu\mathbf{R}\cdot\mathbf{T}}$ that links radial and angular variables is expanded in modified spherical Bessel functions and real spherical harmonics, and the expansion terminates rigorously at $l=p_x+p_y+p_z$, where the $p$'s are the Cartesian powers arising from the Hermite expansion. The angular average is then exact, the atomic limit reduces to a finite sum of terms $C_iR^{n_i}e^{-\mu R^2}$, and the radial moments $\int_0^\infty R^nI(R)\,dR$ are given in closed form through the confluent hypergeometric function ${}_1F_1$. The scheme is exact in principle and fails only arithmetically: we identify the catastrophic cancellations in the angular-momentum coupling that ruin binary64 evaluations for heavy atoms and remove them by elevating the cancelling chain to binary128. Sum rules for the total, Coulomb and exchange-correlation intracules are recovered to seven to eight significant digits for systems from LiH to Kr$_2$, whereas Euler-Maclaurin and Lebedev quadratures err by up to 22% for stretched or multicenter molecules.

papers.title: Spin-Adapted Neural-Network Backflow Wavefunctions for Excited States of Strongly Correlated Open-Shell Systems
authors: Bohan Zhang (Key Laboratory of Theoretical and Computational Photochemistry
Zibo Wu (Key Laboratory of Theoretical and Computational Photochemistry
Yunzhi Li (Key Laboratory of Theoretical and Computational Photochemistry
Wei-Hai Fang (Key Laboratory of Theoretical and Computational Photochemistry
Zhendong Li (Key Laboratory of Theoretical and Computational Photochemistry
papers.abstract: Building on the success of neural-network quantum states (NQS) for molecular ground states, multi-state frameworks such as natural excited states (NES) [Pfau et al., Science 2024, 385, eadn0137] extend NQS to chemically important excited states. However, without control over total spin, such calculations can require the inclusion of many intervening states of other spins, particularly in strongly correlated systems with dense low-energy spectra. We therefore generalize our previously developed spin-adapted neural network backflow (SA-NNBF) ansatz [Li et al., arXiv:2604.06841 (2026)] to improve its variational flexibility for excited-state calculations within a prescribed spin sector. We establish the universality of this extended ansatz within the chosen orbital space and spin sector, and use numerical benchmarks to assess how parameter allocation affects the ansatz's accuracy. With the spin-adapted ansatz, we are able to directly optimize the first excited state (a singlet) of $O_2$ without using any multi-state frameworks. Combining the extended ansatz with NES, we obtain low-lying triplet states of $O_2$ and singlet states of the $[\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{S}_2(\mathrm{SCH}_3)_4]^{2-}$ cluster without including intervening states of other spins. Both the single-state and NES calculations achieve chemical accuracy relative to the exact energies. Our work provides a practical NQS framework for targeting excited states of prescribed spin in strongly correlated systems.

papers.title: Second-Order Polarization Propagator Approximation to the Quadratic Unitary Coupled Cluster Framework I: First-Order Properties
papers.abstract: We have developed a new formulation for calculating first-order properties in the quadratic unitary coupled-cluster singles and doubles (qUCCSD) method, using a second-order polarizable propagator approximation. The accuracy and reliability of this new framework of the proposed approach have been assessed through the calculation of ground- and excited-state dipole moments and oscillator strengths for a set of small molecules. The Hermiticity of the UCC similarity-transformed Hamiltonian allows molecular properties to be evaluated without introducing left-hand eigenvectors, thereby simplifying the theoretical formulation and computational procedure. Furthermore, the proposed formulation preserves the size-intensivity of transition moments, a property that is not generally guaranteed within the conventional non-Hermitian equation-of-motion coupled-cluster framework. To assess the performance of the proposed method, we have benchmarked both ground- and excited-state properties for 11 small molecules against the extrapolated full configuration interaction (exFCI) reference values and compared with the conventional coupled cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) and third-order algebraic diagrammatic construction (ADC(3)) results. The qUCCSD method yields average errors comparable to those of CCSD while demonstrating significantly improved accuracy over the ADC(3) method.

papers.title: The MC-QTAIM: Why, How, and When?
papers.abstract: The multi-component quantum theory of atoms in molecules (MC-QTAIM) generalizes the original QTAIM framework developed by Richard Bader and colleagues, extending atoms-in-molecules analysis beyond ab initio electronic wavefunctions. MC-QTAIM facilitates the examination of the AIM structure in systems and states that require MC wavefunctions, which describe systems containing multiple distinguishable classes of quantum particles. This advancement broadens the applicability of AIM analysis to a wide range of quantum systems and states that were previously inaccessible. These include exotic molecules, such as positronic species; exotic quantum states, such as superposed proton states in molecules with two- or multi-well potential energy surfaces; and non-adiabatic states of conventional molecules. In this review, I aim to explain the fundamental principles of MC-QTAIM analysis in accessible language and explore some of its potential applications. Additionally, the general formalism for energy partitioning in MC systems, called MC Interacting Quantum Atoms (MC-IQA), is introduced. This scheme unifies the energy partitioning of numerous quantum systems and encompasses the IQA method originally developed by Pendas and colleagues, as well as the previously developed two-component IQA (TC-IQA) scheme - developed by our group to analyze positronic systems - as special cases.

papers.title: Perturbative Recovery of Stabilizer-Subspace Correlations for Quantum Computational Chemistry
papers.abstract: Stabilizer-based subspace methods can substantially reduce the quantum resources required for electronic structure calculations, but the resulting projection neglects Hamiltonian couplings to configurations outside the retained subspace. In this work, we introduce Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT) to recover the associated correlation contributions, using the Contextual Subspace Variational Quantum Eigensolver (CS-VQE) as a representative application. The central idea is to exploit the Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection as perturbative operators that generate an external manifold from the optimized reference state. Their energetic contributions are evaluated using an Epstein-Nesbet-type second-order correction or a resolvent-based formulation that retains couplings within the external space. By exploiting the factorized structure of the stabilizer-constrained reference state, the required matrix elements can be evaluated through Pauli expectation values on the reduced contextual register without explicitly reconstructing the full-space wave function. Molecular benchmarks demonstrate substantial reductions in projection-induced energy errors, allowing chemical precision to be achieved with fewer contextual qubits in several cases. These results establish stabilizer-guided perturbation theory as a promising strategy for improving the accuracy of resource-efficient quantum chemistry calculations.

papers.title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
papers.abstract: We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from $\mathcal{O}(N_s)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_s)$, where $N_s$ is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e.\ distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.

papers.title: Efficient targeting of arbitrary excited states with quantum inverse power iteration through filtering polynomials
papers.abstract: In this work, we introduce a quantum inverse power iteration (QIPI) algorithm based on the quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) to target arbitrary excited states. Given an energy shift $\omega$, QIPI prepares the target excited state by iteratively applying an approximation of the shifted inverse Hamiltonian $(H-\omega I)^{-1}$ to a trial state. Prior quantum inverse power approaches typically relied on Fourier decompositions of the inverse Hamiltonian, with numerical quadrature used to reconstruct the transformation, but such methods are highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices and have been observed to be numerically unstable, effectively restricting their use to ground-state preparation. To enable robust excited-state targeting, we investigate two alternative transformation techniques: a Chebyshev decomposition of the inverse (Cheb-inv) and an eigenstate filtering (EF) approach based on QSVT. We find that EF-based QIPI is substantially more robust than Cheb-inv and other decomposition-based approaches due to the symmetry of the applied filtering polynomial, avoiding divergence with respect to the choice of $\omega$ and efficiently suppressing off-target eigenstates even in closely spaced spectra. Numerical simulations for molecular Hamiltonians of H$_2$, LiH, and BeH$_2$ show improved convergence and enhanced access to higher excited states relative to other quantum power methods. Assuming standard oracle access to the Hamiltonian, we further provide logical resource estimates in fault-tolerant settings in terms of T gate counts, and conclude that QIPI can achieve high target state amplification with modest polynomial degrees, thereby making it a promising candidate for scalable excited-state preparation in fault-tolerant quantum chemistry applications.

papers.title: Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.

papers.title: Implementation of Girsanov Reweighting in CP2K
papers.abstract: Dynamical reweighting of path measures is a powerful approach for accurately evaluating slow molecular processes using modified potential energy surfaces used in enhanced sampling methods. Integrating this reweighting framework into the CP2K electronic-structure and molecular-dynamics (MD) software package delivers a robust and widely applicable tool for metadynamics, uncertainty quantification, and force-field optimisation based on both \textit{ab initio} and classical MD simulations. Based on the Girsanov theorem for stochastic dynamical systems, the method is adapted to the Bussi-Donadio-Parrinello velocity-rescaling scheme. This scheme is accessible through the CSVR thermostat and can be interpreted as a Langevin OVRVO/OBABO update scheme requiring two random numbers per integration step. Comprehensive implementation details are provided, including a complete overview of the modified CP2K modules involved in the MD cycle and the computation of reweighting factors. The framework supports multiple sources of bias potentials, enabling reweighting via the PLUMED interface or CP2K-native external potentials and restraints. The feasibility of the implementation is demonstrated through rerun benchmarks, dynamical reweighting of Markov state models (MSMs) and computation of transport properties based on CP2K trajectories, showing excellent agreement with reference simulations.
